summary_paragraph: A 70-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, hypertension, osteoporosis with multiple compression fractures, and chronic back pain was admitted for a two-day history of dry cough exacerbating her chronic back pain. She had no fever, shortness of breath, or signs of heart failure. Initial chest X-ray showed low lung volumes and interstitial edema. CT chest revealed no pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or interstitial lung disease, but showed bibasilar atelectasis and small bilateral pleural effusions. Her persistent oxygen requirement was attributed to splinting from thoracic pain and kyphosis. The cough was diagnosed as acute viral bronchitis, and treatments initiated in the ED were discontinued as they were not indicated. Pain management was optimized with lidocaine patches, acetaminophen, tramadol, and continued gabapentin. Chronic pancytopenia was noted but remained stable and was deemed non-urgent. She improved clinically and was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with a plan for outpatient follow-up.
